title: From outsider to ancestor (Ruth 4)
hook: the Moabite woman becomes the great-grandmother of King David
tomorrow: A man in the land of Uz

segments.voice: Yesterday, Boaz told his workers to drop a little extra grain where Ruth was gleaning. Your line was let fall some handfuls. What did you leave behind for someone else to find? Today, the last chapter of Ruth. Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

The book of Ruth ends with a list of names. But before the list, there's a morning at the city gate. Boaz goes up and sits down there, the place where a town did its business. A relative of Naomi's walks by, a nearer kinsman than Boaz, and Boaz calls him over. He gathers elders of the city as witnesses. Then he lays it out: Naomi is selling a piece of land, and the nearer kinsman has the first right to buy it back. Sure, the man says, I'll redeem it. Then Boaz adds the rest. The land comes with Ruth, the Moabite widow, and with keeping her late husband's name alive. The man backs out. He pulls off his shoe and hands it over, the old way of sealing a deal, and the field and the future pass to Boaz.
screen: `A MORNING AT THE CITY GATE.` → `THE NEARER KINSMAN BACKS OUT.` → `A SHOE SEALS THE DEAL.`

segments.voice: Notice what the book keeps calling her, right up to the end. Not Ruth the wife of Boaz. Ruth the Moabitess. Back in chapter two she called herself a foreigner, and the story never pretends otherwise. She marries Boaz, and a son is born. And then the camera swings away from the parents to Naomi. Naomi, who came home empty and asked to be called bitter. The women of Bethlehem gather around her and praise Ruth to her face. In the King James words, they call her "thy daughter in law, which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons." Seven sons, said to a woman who buried two. Naomi takes the baby and lays him in her lap and cares for him. Then the neighbors give him a name, and here's the line the whole book has been walking toward: "There is a son born to Naomi; and they called his name Obed: he is the father of Jesse, the father of David." David. His great-grandmother came from Moab, a people the Torah elsewhere keeps out of the assembly. The rabbis noticed that tension. The Talmud records a reading that the old rule names Moabite men, not Moabite women, which left a door open for Ruth. The book itself just ends with the family line, generation by generation, and the last name on it is David. Tradition reads this book on Shavuot, the festival of receiving the Torah, and some readers hear why: Ruth chose to come in. A story that began with a famine and three graves ends with a cradle and a king. The outsider was never made to stop being an outsider. She became an ancestor anyway.
screen: `STILL CALLED RUTH THE MOABITESS.` · `BETTER THAN SEVEN SONS.` · `A SON BORN TO NAOMI.` · then, large: `THE FATHER OF JESSE, THE FATHER OF DAVID.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor an outsider in your story. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who came into your family or your life from somewhere else. A stepparent. An in-law. A grandparent who arrived in a new country with a suitcase. A neighbor who became family. Hold their face for a moment. Then ask: what came into my life through them? A recipe, a word, a way of holding a baby, a reason I'm here at all. Let the breath carry their name in and out. If you pray, you can name them before God with thanks. The bell holds the time.
Moabitess, what the book keeps calling Ruth even after she becomes the great-grandmother of King David. Today's word.
Your line: a cradle and a king. Today, say out loud, to someone or to yourself, the name of one person who came in from outside and changed your family's story. Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish communities read the book of Ruth on the festival of Shavuot, and Ruth is remembered in Jewish tradition as a woman who chose to join the Jewish people and as an ancestor of King David.

fork.reveal: he backs out and pulls off his shoe to seal it. the man who said no is never named, and the family line goes through Boaz and Ruth to David.

notes: Ruth 4:2 says Boaz took ten elders; the script says 'elders' without the number.
'Lays him in her lap': KJV 4:16 has 'laid it in her bosom, and became nurse unto it'; paraphrased.

The Moabite exclusion is Deuteronomy 23:4 in Jewish numbering (23:3 in KJV). Yevamot 76b reading 'Moabite, not Moabitess' (Amoni velo Amonit, Moavi velo Moavit) is paraphrased; please confirm the citation and phrasing.

Reading Ruth on Shavuot is stated as tradition; the reason given (Ruth chose to come in) is attributed to 'some readers'. Other reasons are also given in tradition (harvest setting, David's yahrzeit).
'Three graves' refers to Elimelech, Mahlon and Chilion (Ruth 1:3–5).
Original: נָכְרִיָּה from Ruth 2:10; please confirm the vocalization.
Editor: added Ruth 1:1–5 to sources so the famine, the three graves and 'a woman who buried two' sons are backed by a cited text; spoken lines unchanged.
